title: Remarks: A Reset on Liquidity Regulation
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, through Under Secretary Jonathan McKernan, outlined a comprehensive review of post-2008 bank liquidity regulation, arguing that current frameworks unnecessarily constrain lending capacity as the U.S. seeks to finance massive infrastructure investments in AI, domestic manufacturing, and defense. The remarks signal Treasury's intent to revisit the balance between requiring banks to self-insure liquidity risk versus utilizing the lender of last resort, particularly addressing issues of discount window stigma and buffer usability that became apparent during the March 2023 banking stress.
key_points: Post-2008 liquidity regulation was described as 'novel and even muddled guesswork' with 'two parts data, one part gut, and a heavy dash of post-crisis trauma'
Large banks now allocate approximately 25% of balance sheets to safe assets, up from roughly 10% pre-crisis, constraining lending capacity

The March 2023 banking stress (SVB, Signature, First Republic) exposed that bank liquidity existed 'only on paper' because collateral was not fully prepositioned and discount window access was untested

Treasury argues that both regulators and markets have treated liquidity buffers as 'untouchable hard minimums' rather than shock absorbers, which paradoxically exacerbates liquidity stress transmission
The framework has entrenched discount window stigma by incentivizing banks to exhaust regulatory buffers before accessing central bank facilities
Treasury will propose modernization of bank capital that 'simplifies and rationalizes the framework, ends the capital arbitrage that drives financial activity to nonbanks'
why_it_matters: This speech signals a significant policy shift in bank liquidity regulation that could free up hundreds of billions to potentially trillions of dollars in lending capacity. For market participants, changes to liquidity buffer requirements could alter bank balance sheet allocation patterns, affect demand for Treasuries and agency MBS, and reshape the functioning of the discount window and central bank lending facilities. The framing around reducing moral hazard concerns while restoring the lender of last resort to its 'intended role' suggests potential structural changes to how liquidity stress events are managed.
macro_context: Treasury explicitly links liquidity regulatory reform to financing needs for AI infrastructure, domestic supply chains, and defense industrial base—framing this as necessary to support a broader economic transformation. The speech connects regulatory easing to broader fiscal and economic policy objectives under the current administration.
market_structure_context: The remarks directly address market structure issues: (1) buffer usability and the paradox where hard minimum buffers can accelerate rather than absorb liquidity stress; (2) discount window stigma and the need to normalize central bank facility access; (3) the role of large banks as 'liquidity insurers' for the financial system being described as a mistake; (4) the distinction that only the central bank can create new reserves to add aggregate system-wide base liquidity. Treasury signals intent to propose reforms to restore the lender of last resort to its intended role and incentivize collateral prepositioning.
